questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Define the term crystallographic axes.

(3 marks)

(ii) Describe the variation shown by the crystallographic axes within the various crystal systems.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Crystallographic axes.** Crystallographic axes are **imaginary straight reference lines that pass through the centre of an ideal crystal** and meet there. They are used to describe the **orientation and position of the crystal faces**: each face is defined by the **intercepts** (lengths) it cuts on the axes, and the crystal system is defined by the **number of axes, their relative lengths and the angles between them**. The three axes (hexagonal system: four) are labelled $a$, $b$ and $c$ (with $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ and $c$ in the hexagonal system), and the angles between them are $\alpha$ (between $b$ and $c$), $\beta$ (between $a$ and $c$) and $\gamma$ (between $a$ and $b$).

**(ii) Variation of the axes in the crystal systems.** The six crystal systems (the trigonal system is treated here as a division of the hexagonal system; some books count seven systems) differ in the **number of axes, in whether their lengths are equal and in the angles between them**:

| System | Axes and lengths | Angles between the axes | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cubic (isometric) | three axes, **all equal**: $a = b = c$ | all $90^\circ$ ($\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 90^\circ$) | halite, galena, pyrite, fluorite, garnet |
| Tetragonal | three axes, **two equal** horizontal axes and a third (vertical) of different length: $a = b \neq c$ | all $90^\circ$ | zircon, rutile, cassiterite |
| Orthorhombic | three axes, **all unequal**: $a \neq b \neq c$ | all $90^\circ$ | olivine, topaz, barytes, sulphur |
| Monoclinic | three axes, **all unequal** | $\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ$ but $\beta \neq 90^\circ$ (two axes are oblique, the third is perpendicular to both) | gypsum, orthoclase, muscovite, augite, hornblende |
| Triclinic | three axes, **all unequal** | **none** is $90^\circ$ ($\alpha \neq \beta \neq \gamma \neq 90^\circ$) | plagioclase feldspars, microcline, kyanite |
| Hexagonal (with trigonal) | **four** axes: three equal horizontal axes $a_1 = a_2 = a_3$ in one plane and a fourth, $c$, of different length perpendicular to them | the three horizontal axes are $120^\circ$ apart; $c$ is $90^\circ$ to them | beryl, apatite, quartz and calcite (trigonal) |

So the variation is shown in three ways: (1) **three axes in all systems except the hexagonal, which has four**; (2) the axes may be **all equal (cubic), two equal (tetragonal, and the three horizontal axes of the hexagonal system) or all unequal (orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic)**; (3) the angles may be **all $90^\circ$ (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic), have one oblique angle (monoclinic), have no right angle (triclinic) or be $120^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ (hexagonal)**. The symmetry of the crystal decreases from the cubic system (highest symmetry) to the triclinic system (lowest).

**Sketches to draw:** a set of three axes at right angles with equal lengths (cubic); the same with a longer or shorter vertical $c$ (tetragonal); three unequal axes at right angles (orthorhombic); the inclined $a$ axis with angle $\beta$ (monoclinic); three oblique unequal axes (triclinic); and the four-axis hexagonal cross with the three horizontal axes at $120^\circ$. Label $a$, $b$, $c$ and the angles on each.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Differentiate between the terms polymorphism and pseudomorphism as used in mineralogy, stating ONE example in each case.

(6 marks)

(ii) What is a Solid Solution Series?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Polymorphism and pseudomorphism.**

**Polymorphism** is the property by which a substance of **one and the same chemical composition crystallises in two or more different crystal structures** (often different crystal systems), the forms being called **polymorphs**. The structure formed depends on the **conditions of temperature and pressure** (and sometimes the presence of impurities) at the time of crystallisation, and the polymorphs have **different physical properties** (hardness, density, cleavage, colour). *Example:* **carbon**, $\mathrm{C}$, occurs as **diamond** (cubic, hardness 10, very dense, formed at very high pressure in the mantle) and as **graphite** (hexagonal, hardness 1 to 2, soft, formed at lower pressure). Other examples are calcite and aragonite ($\mathrm{CaCO_3}$) and the three $\mathrm{Al_2SiO_5}$ minerals kyanite, andalusite and sillimanite.

**Pseudomorphism** is the occurrence of a mineral **in the external crystal form of another mineral** which it has **replaced**. The original mineral is **chemically altered, dissolved or replaced** (or its mould is filled), but the **outward shape of the original crystal is kept** while the **composition and internal structure are those of the new mineral**. It forms by replacement (substitution), by alteration, by incrustation or by infilling of a mould. *Example:* **limonite after pyrite**: cubes of pyrite ($\mathrm{FeS_2}$) altered by oxidation to iron oxide hydroxide, so that the cube shape of pyrite is kept but the substance is limonite (another example: malachite after azurite).

**Difference in short.** In polymorphism the **composition is the same but the structure and the crystal form differ**; in pseudomorphism the **crystal form is the same as that of the old mineral but the composition is different** (it is a new mineral in an old shape).

**(ii) Solid Solution Series.** A solid solution series is a group of minerals which have the **same basic crystal structure**, in which **one ion can substitute for another ion of similar size and charge** (ionic radii within about 15 per cent) in the lattice, so that the **chemical composition varies continuously between two or more end members** without any change in the structure. The substitution may be simple (same charge) or **coupled** (the charge is balanced by a second substitution). The properties (density, refractive index, colour) vary regularly with composition. The temperature of crystallisation also controls the extent of the substitution.

*Examples:* (1) the **olivine series**, from forsterite $\mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4}$ to fayalite $\mathrm{Fe_2SiO_4}$, in which $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ replace each other (the **continuous branch of Bowen's reaction series**); (2) the **plagioclase feldspar series**, from albite $\mathrm{NaAlSi_3O_8}$ to anorthite $\mathrm{CaAl_2Si_2O_8}$, by the coupled substitution $\mathrm{Na^+ + Si^{4+}} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{Ca^{2+} + Al^{3+}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) State the sources and the main uses of clay.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Clay** is a very fine-grained (less than 0.002 mm) natural material, made mainly of **clay minerals** (hydrated aluminium silicates such as kaolinite, illite and montmorillonite), which is **plastic when wet** and hardens when dried and fired.

**Sources of clay.**

1. **Chemical weathering (hydrolysis) of silicate minerals, especially feldspars**, in granites, gneisses, basalts and other rocks, in warm, wet (humid tropical) climates, which gives **residual clays** (kaolin and laterite clays) lying on the parent rock.
2. **Hydrothermal alteration** of feldspar-rich rocks by hot waters, which gives pure kaolin deposits.
3. **Transport and deposition** of clay particles by rivers, wind and ice into lakes, lagoons, floodplains, deltas and sea basins, which gives **sedimentary clays** and, after compaction, mudstones and **shales**.
4. **Alteration of volcanic ash and glass**, which gives **bentonite** (montmorillonite).

**Main uses of clay.**

1. **Bricks, tiles, pipes and building blocks** (burnt or sun-dried), and **pottery, earthenware, stoneware and porcelain** (ceramics; kaolin for fine porcelain and sanitary ware).
2. **Cement manufacture** (clay or shale is heated with limestone) and **refractory bricks** for furnaces.
3. **Filler and coating** in paper, paints, rubber and plastics (kaolin).
4. **Drilling mud** in oil and water wells (bentonite) and **foundry moulds**.
5. **Waterproof liners and cores** of dams, ponds and waste dumps (very low permeability), and **absorbents** and fuller's earth for purifying oils, cat litter and carriers in medicines, cosmetics and agrochemicals.
